droppedAngles.title: security
droppedAngles.why: Checked the timer entry point, account serialization, environment use, and changed storage field. The job consumes no untrusted request data, introduces no network sink, secret handling, redirect, injection surface, or public exposure of lastAccruedOn; authorization and machine attribution remain separately in scope.

scoutNotes: This PR adds an account-level lastAccruedOn field and migration, then changes interest accrual to skip accounts whose marker matches the computed current day. It also starts an hourly unref'ed accrual-and-save timer when src/server.js is executed directly and updates documentation and tests for same-day idempotency.

confirmed.title: Local and UTC days diverge
confirmed.rootCause: Accrual compares a host-local calendar day but persists the UTC calendar day, breaking the duplicate-credit guard when those dates differ.
confirmed.summary: The duplicate check uses the host-local calendar day while the stored marker uses the UTC day, so there is no consistent bank timezone.
confirmed.failure: With TZ=Asia/Colombo and an open account holding 100000 cents at 500 bps, calls at 2026-03-02T18:45:00Z and 2026-03-02T19:45:00Z both regard the local day as 2026-03-03 but persist lastAccruedOn as 2026-03-02. Both calls credit 13 cents, leaving 100026 cents instead of 100013.

sites.title: Day marker disagrees with skip date

confirmed.reasoning: The server scheduler and CLI job call accrueInterest without any guard or timezone normalization, and deployment documentation imposes no UTC timezone invariant. The function compares date.toLocaleDateString('en-CA'), which uses the process-local timezone, against lastAccruedOn written from date.toISOString().slice(0, 10), which is UTC. Running the stated reproduction under TZ=Asia/Colombo showed localDay 2026-03-03 and stored marker 2026-03-02 at both 2026-03-02T18:45Z and 19:45Z; both calls credited 13 cents, producing a 100026-cent balance. The full 35-test suite passed because the added test uses noon UTC, outside the divergent-date window.
confirmed.panel: 3 of 3 skeptics could not refute it

confirmed.title: Cutover recredits already-paid accounts
confirmed.rootCause: Migration 004 initializes every legacy account as never accrued, allowing accounts already credited on the rollout day to be credited again.
confirmed.summary: Migration 004 marks every existing account as uncredited even when the previous scheduler already paid that day's interest.
confirmed.failure: A legacy account already credited on the rollout day is migrated with lastAccruedOn:null and receives a second daily credit when the new server timer first runs that day.
confirmed.reasoning: Migration 004 unconditionally assigns null when lastAccruedOn is absent and examines neither audit entries nor the rollout date. accrueInterest skips only an exact match with today. A version-3 account at 100013 with a same-day interest audit entry migrated to lastAccruedOn:null; accrual on 2026-03-02 then credited 13 cents again, producing 100026. Existing tests cover repeated runs after the new marker has been written, not upgraded accounts.

confirmed.title: Hourly save races request saves
confirmed.rootCause: Background accrual saves are not serialized with request saves, allowing concurrent whole-file writes to race through the same temporary path.
confirmed.summary: The hourly callback launches an unserialized save while request handlers may save concurrently, and both writes use the same process-specific temporary filename.
confirmed.failure: When the hourly save and a deposit save overlap, the request's save can reject with ENOENT after the deposit mutation; the route returns 500, and retrying against the still-mutated process credits and audits the deposit again.
confirmed.reasoning: The timer invokes store.save() without coordination with request handlers, and every save uses the same PID-based temporary path. In 20 two-save reproductions, every pair had one ENOENT rename rejection; a further 50-run check rejected one save every time, usually the second invocation. Request mutations occur before their awaited save, so a rejected request can return 500 while retaining the deposit in memory, and a retry applies it again.

confirmed.title: Restart loops prevent all accrual
confirmed.rootCause: The server schedules its first accrual only after one full hour, so frequent restarts can prevent accrual indefinitely.
confirmed.summary: Interest is not run at startup, so the first attempt requires a full uninterrupted hour of server uptime.
confirmed.failure: With no external scheduler and restarts less than one hour apart, no accrual callback runs, so eligible accounts can remain uncredited indefinitely.
confirmed.reasoning: The direct-execution block only registers setInterval and never invokes accrual during startup. Intercepting timer registration showed a 3600000 ms delay and no registration-time callback. Restarting the process sooner destroys the pending timer, and createServer itself contains no scheduler.

confirmed.title: Legacy scheduler remains a concurrent writer
confirmed.rootCause: The quickstart still directs operators to run the legacy external interest scheduler, creating a concurrent whole-file writer alongside the server scheduler.
confirmed.summary: The PR leaves newly obsolete external-scheduler guidance in place, but the external job's ability to overwrite concurrent acknowledged API changes already existed before this diff.
confirmed.failure: If the external job opens the ledger before an API deposit is saved and writes its stale snapshot afterward, the acknowledged deposit is removed from the persisted ledger.

sites.title: Legacy scheduler remains a concurrent writer

confirmed.reasoning: The quickstart still says to run scripts/run-jobs.mjs interest daily. That script opens an independent Store and later rewrites the entire ledger. A two-Store reproduction persisted a deposit balance of 101000, then a stale job save replaced it with 100013. The new daily marker does not coordinate whole-file writes. However, the same quickstart instruction, external script, and whole-file Store.save behavior existed in the parent commit, so this precise stale-overwrite failure predates the PR.

confirmed.title: Clock sampled across midnight
confirmed.rootCause: Accrual samples the clock twice, so a midnight boundary can make the compared day differ from the recorded timestamp's day.
confirmed.summary: Sampling clock separately for the timestamp and day allows one accrual to span midnight and compare against a different day than it records.
confirmed.failure: An invocation whose two clock reads straddle UTC midnight can compare against March 3 but record March 2, allowing both that invocation and the next March 3 invocation to credit interest.
confirmed.reasoning: Under TZ=UTC, I ran accrueInterest with lastAccruedOn='2026-03-02' and a clock returning 2026-03-02T23:59:59.999Z followed by 2026-03-03T00:00:00.001Z. It credited 13 cents while recording lastAccruedOn='2026-03-02'. A subsequent March 3 invocation credited another 13 cents, producing 100026. The two clock calls have no intervening guard, and the fixed-clock test cannot cover this rollover.

confirmed.title: Rollback writes erase accrual marker
confirmed.rootCause: The previous release's schema drops lastAccruedOn during account updates, so rollback or mixed-version writes erase the new marker.
confirmed.summary: The new marker is not compatible with the previous release's projected account schema, so any old-code account update silently deletes it.
confirmed.failure: After release 4 credits an account, a release-3 account update projects away lastAccruedOn and saves version 4. A release-4 restart skips migration 004 and credits that account again on the same calendar day.
confirmed.reasoning: I loaded a version-4 ledger through the actual parent commit's Store implementation, performed an account balance update, and saved it. Parent SCHEMA projection removed lastAccruedOn while retaining data.version=4. Reopening with the PR code caused migrate() to return [], and same-day accrueInterest credited the account again. docs/deploy.md explicitly allows mixed-version copies, and there is no maximum-version compatibility guard.

confirmed.title: Failed accrual remains only in memory
confirmed.rootCause: A failed background save leaves the accrual mutations active only in memory without rollback or immediate durable retry.
confirmed.summary: A failed background save is only logged after balance, marker, and audit mutations remain active in memory, with no rollback or immediate durable retry.
confirmed.failure: If the hourly save rejects and the process exits before another successful save, clients can observe the credited in-memory balance even though disk retains the old balance and marker; restarting on a later day permanently omits the failed day's interest.

sites.title: Failed accrual remains only in memory

confirmed.reasoning: I persisted a 100000-cent account marked March 1, accrued it on March 2, and forced save() to reject. Memory contained balance 100013 and lastAccruedOn March 2, while the file still contained balance 100000 and March 1. Store reads and cache invalidation expose the mutated in-memory row. Reloading the file on March 3 then applied only one 13-cent credit and marked March 3, leaving March 2's credit absent. The timer's rejection handler only logs and neither rolls back nor retries immediately.

confirmed.title: Missed days collapse into one
confirmed.rootCause: The job applies only one day's interest whenever the marker is not today, so it cannot recover multiple missed days.
confirmed.summary: The job only distinguishes today from another date and always applies one daily amount, so it cannot recover calendar days missed during downtime or timer delay.
confirmed.failure: After a Friday marker and weekend downtime, Monday's invocation credits only one day's 13 cents instead of the three daily credits due through Monday, then advances the marker to Monday so the two omitted days cannot be recovered.
confirmed.reasoning: With lastAccruedOn='2026-03-06' and the clock set to Monday 2026-03-09, accrueInterest ran dailyInterest exactly once, added 13 cents, and immediately set lastAccruedOn to March 9. It did not credit Saturday or Sunday. The parent implementation likewise calculated only one day's amount per invocation, so the underlying inability to recover missed executions is pre-existing as claimed.

confirmed.title: Accrual exceptions crash the server
confirmed.rootCause: The interval callback does not catch synchronous exceptions from accrueInterest, allowing an accrual error to terminate the server process.
confirmed.summary: The interval catches only the asynchronous save rejection, so any synchronous exception from accrueInterest escapes the timer callback and terminates the Node process.
confirmed.failure: After one hour, a server using a version-4 ledger whose audit field is null and which contains an eligible interest-bearing account throws synchronously from Store.insert('audit', ...). The exception escapes the interval callback, terminates the process, and leaves the credited balance and lastAccruedOn change unpersisted.
confirmed.reasoning: Store.load() preserves a parsed audit:null value, and migration 004 is skipped for a version-4 ledger. A focused reproduction showed accrueInterest() updated the eligible account from 100000 to 100013 in memory, then record() threw TypeError on null.push; store.save() was never reached and the disk balance remained 100000. Executing the same callback through a timer terminated Node with exit status 1. No uncaughtException handler exists. The normal test suite passed but does not cover malformed loaded collections or timer exception containment.

missed.what: src/server.js:162-165 unconditionally calls store.save() every hour, even when accrueInterest returns zero changes. Because Store.save serializes and rewrites the entire ledger, this creates up to 23 unnecessary full-file rewrites after the day's accrual and performs that work in the HTTP-serving process.
missed.why: No performance or capacity angle examined the I/O amplification and request-latency consequences of moving the batch job into the server; the prior race and failure findings address integrity, not the cost of successful no-op saves.
